1.title: An Anthology of Twenty-Two Voices, Opening at the Fire
1.synthesis:
Maṇḍala 1 is the largest book of the Ṛgveda — 191 sūktas, 2,006 ṛcs — and it is not one family's book. The six maṇḍalas that follow each belong to a single lineage. This one is an anthology: twenty-two ṛṣis arranged in twenty-five blocks, gathered from many families and set at the head of the collection. Reading it in order means reading through one household's voice, then another's.

The blocks are long enough to have character. {{madhucchandas}} opens with ten sūktas, and his are the shortest and plainest — the first ten hymns of the Ṛgveda are also among its most compact. {{gotama}} holds twenty at [[1.74]]–[[1.93]]; {{kutsa}} twenty more; and {{dīrghatamas}} the longest unbroken stretch in the collection, twenty-five sūktas at [[1.140]]–[[1.164]], ending in the Riddle Hymn. {{agastya}} closes the book with the last twenty-seven, and his own signature line seals twenty-one of them. Six sūktas, [[1.65]] to [[1.70]], run in *virāṭ*, and the metre is short enough that both translators merge pairs of ṛcs into single English units — 5 rows for the tradition's 10. ([[1.149]] is in *virāṭ* too and is not halved, so the metre alone does not force it; there the ṛcs are already few.)

Two gods hold the book. {{indra}} takes 50 sūktas and 519 ṛcs; {{agni}} 47 and 427. Together they are half of it. But the shape underneath is the same one the whole collection uses: the book opens at [[1.1]] with Agni, as every family book opens with Agni, because he is the one who carries what is given. Then {{aśvin}} — 18 sūktas, 229 ṛcs, more than their share elsewhere, concentrated in {{kakṣīvān}}'s block and again at the close — and {{marut}}, {{uṣas}}, {{viśvedevā}}.

What the book emphasises is the daily rite and its whole cast. Agni kindled before dawn; {{uṣas}} arriving; the {{soma}} pressed and offered to {{vāyu}} first, then Indra; the {{āp}}, the waters, invoked as healers; {{mitrāvaruṇā}} holding the order of day and night. Read across the blocks, the same morning recurs in a dozen households' words.

And the book knows how to end. Its last long stretch turns strange — a dialogue between Indra and the {{marut}}s over who killed Vṛtra, a quarrel between Indra and Agastya, Lopāmudrā telling her husband the waiting is done, the Riddle Hymn asking what holds the unborn up, a hymn to food itself, and a charm against poison. A book that opened with a priest asking Agni for wealth closes with a woman arguing, a riddle nobody answers, and a cure for snakebite.
1.practice:
**Why anything is poured into fire at all.** This is the question the book answers first, and the answer is structural rather than devotional. Agni is the only god who is physically present — burning on the hearth, visible, in the room. Everything else is elsewhere. So what is given to the gods has to be given *through* him: poured into the fire, transformed by it, and carried up. That is why he is called *hotā*, the one who offers or calls, and *dūta*, the messenger, and why the very first line of the collection names him four times over by function. The rite is not a symbol of contact. It is the mechanism of it, and fire is the part of the mechanism you can see.

This is also why Agni is still the witness of the saṃskāras — circled at a wedding, kindled at the upanayana, lit at the last rite. The addressee has not changed in three thousand years, and the logic has not either.

**The waters.** {{āp}} run through 105 verses of this maṇḍala. They are invoked as *mātaraḥ*, mothers, and as carrying *bheṣaja*, medicine — [[1.23]] asks them plainly for healing, and the same hymn calls them purifiers of what the rite has touched. The waters are not scenery: they are what makes a thing fit to offer, and what makes a body well. Every ācamana before a rite, and every invocation of the waters at a saṃskāra, is downstream of this.

**{{ṛta}}** appears in 71 verses here — the same count as in maṇḍala 10, and seven times what maṇḍala 2 carries. It is the order that makes the seasons turn and a promise hold, and the same word for the sacrifice. To act in accordance with it and to perform the rite correctly are not two things.

**What to read first.** [[1.1]] for why fire; [[1.23]] for the waters; [[1.32]] for Indra and Vṛtra; [[1.113]] for Uṣas; [[1.114]] for Rudra; [[1.164]] when you want the book to stop explaining and start asking.
1.disagreements:
Maṇḍala 1 is generally held to be a later addition to the collection, along with maṇḍala 10 — the family books II–VII form the older core, and this anthology was assembled around them. The evidence is structural rather than doctrinal: the family books each carry one lineage, while this one carries twenty-two ṛṣis in blocks, and it shares its size (191 sūktas) exactly with maṇḍala 10, the other late book.

The arrangement within it is mechanical, and demonstrably so. Across the family books, 32 of 36 multi-hymn deity blocks run by decreasing verse count — sort by deity, Agni first, then longest to shortest. That is a filing rule, not a narrative, and this book follows it inside each ṛṣi's block.

Sāyaṇa, writing under Vijayanagara patronage around 1360, glossed the whole of it, and his bhāṣya is the reading most of the tradition inherited. Where his gloss survives in this witness it appears beneath each verse. Wilson translates following him throughout; Griffith translates independently, and the two diverge most where the tradition's ritual reading parts company with 19th-century philology.
